description_full: Leidos Holdings, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides services and solutions for government and commercial customers in the United States and internationally. The National Security & Digital segment provides national security software; services by using artificial intelligence and machine learning to coordinate sea, ground, air, and space to help warfighters; offensive, defensive, and physical cyber operation solutions; intelligence analysis, operational support, logistics operations, security, linguistics, force production, biometrics, chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosives, energetics, training, and other services; and Digital Modernization and transformation services. The Health & Civil segment offers air traffic control systems; health mission software; managed health services; infrastructure management and operation; logistical operations and information technology support; and life science research and development support services. The Commercial & International segment provides power grid engineering and design, grid modernization, utility planning and consulting, energy management and efficiency, technology-driven innovation, and software and application development; people scanners, computed tomography carry-on baggage scanners, checked baggage scanners, and explosive trace detectors; mobile, non-intrusive ports and borders inspection systems; and open-architecture platform that transforms airport security by integrating disparate devices and technologies into a unified management system. The Defense Systems segment offers air and missile defense, maritime, aerospace, and cyber and threat systems; offers airborne training, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions; and provides space-based electro-optic infrared systems, multi/hyperspectral, electronic warfare and signals intelligence, and communications payloads. Leidos Holdings, Inc. was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in Reston, Virginia.

financial_summary: Leidos Holdings, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $16.2B market cap on $17.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $1.6B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.21× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.6×.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Significant goodwill (47% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (35% annualized) adds uncertainty

Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 5pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.52x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 39% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 35% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.80, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $141.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 21% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $284, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 54%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $217 to $387 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 11.9 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 9.4 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 10.0 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 32% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $152 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.75).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.21x.
ROE of 29% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1B of cash against $4.6B of debt), with interest covered 9.6x.
Goodwill makes up 47% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.1% over 3 years, 6.9% over 5 years and 13.0% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
At current returns, reinvesting 65% of profits supports about 7.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.13 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.1x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 3%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 87%.
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (2.5% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years.
people: With about 50,000 employees, each generates about $343K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 3.1% a year.
That works out to $32K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.6M (13x revenue per employee).
